A complex of solar power plants near Ouarzazate, on the edge of the Sahara in southern Morocco, built from 2013 to 2018. Noor means light in Arabic. It is one of the largest concentrated solar power stations in the world.

Most of its plants do not use ordinary solar panels. Instead, some two million mirrors focus sunlight to heat a fluid, which makes steam to drive turbines. Heat stored in tanks of molten salt lets the plant keep producing power for hours after sunset. One plant uses curved troughs of mirrors; another, a tall tower that the mirrors aim at. A smaller section uses panels.

Morocco has almost no oil or gas of its own and imported nearly all its energy. King Mohammed VI opened the first plant in 2016. The project was paid for by Moroccan funds and loans from the World Bank, European and African lenders. It is part of Morocco's plan to make about half its power capacity renewable by 2030, and revived old dreams of North African sun powering Europe as well.
